newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - Axa Equity & Law sale.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - Axa Equity & Law sale.

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN
No real surprises in reports in the UK press today that Axa is planning to sell life insurer Axa Equity & Law in the wake of its merger with UAP.

It has never been clear how Equity & Law would coexist with Sun Life and Provincial - 60% owned by UAP. Cost savings through rationalisation might have come from pooling the two companies in an all share merger, but many observers thought the two firms too similar to be a perfect strategic fit: they both operate multi-distribution channels, although they are both heavily reliant on the independent financial advisor market.

Both reported very similar levels of new life business in 1995 - around 63m (100% of regular premiums, plus 10% of single premiums); but Sun Life is way ahead on pensions business - over 100m of new premiums in 1995 compared with 35m from Equity & Law.

Selling one of the companies was always an option if a good price could be obtained. And lo and behold, conditions for that are ideal. The interest in Scottish Amicable, which now has six officially interested parties looking at it, has focused attention on the sector, and will inevitably raise the value of alternative purchases for the losers on the Scot Am deal.

In fact Proteus can't help wondering whether a sale was not the post-merger plan from the beginning. Plans to replace the name AXA equity & Law to AXA Life in November quietly disappeared, and an enhanced press team upped the profile of the company, now more often referred to as Equity & Law.

But most interesting is to wonder what was said to Mark Wood, the former AA Insurance managing director who was brought in to head Equity & Law only days before the AXA-UAP merger was announced. Did he really arrive in his new office to find the picture had completely changed? Or was he briefed on the upcoming move and on his role in spinning off the life unit?

Woods' appointment surprised the UK market. He significantly increased profits in AA's insurance broking, credit card and financing activities. Part of this he did by introducing new computer systems and other efficiency measures. But also during that time scores of AA retail outlets were closed and more than 2000 jobs axed. AXA denied at the time he was coming in to do a similar job, but it could well be that from the start he has been a man with a mission.
